_note: Every orbital figure here was retrieved from the NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP service, table pscomppars (Planetary Systems Composite Parameters), on 2026-08-19. Nothing is estimated, rounded from memory, or invented. Where the archive returned no value the field is null and the confidence is lowered accordingly. These are SPATIAL TEMPLATES: the geometry is borrowed, the meaning comes from Siddhesh's graph.

systems.geometryBasis: Extremely compact resonant chain. All seven orbits lie inside 0.062 AU — the whole system would fit well inside Mercury's orbit. Spacing ratio outer/inner = 5.4.
systems.visualCharacter: dense, tightly nested, near-equal spacing, everything close to the star
systems.notes: Complete measured geometry for all 7 planets.

systems.geometryBasis: Directly imaged, enormously wide. Outer planet is 4.1x the inner. Spans 16-68 AU.
systems.visualCharacter: vast, sparse, four widely separated bodies, huge negative space
systems.notes: The strongest available contrast to TRAPPIST-1.

systems.geometryBasis: Extreme dynamic range: an ultra-short-period planet at 0.015 AU and a distant giant at 5.6 AU — a 363x span.
systems.visualCharacter: one body almost touching the star, then a huge leap outward
systems.notes: Archive reports sy_pnum 7 but returned geometry for only 5. Two planets lack values in pscomppars.

systems.geometryBasis: Strikingly regular near-geometric progression — each orbit roughly 2x the previous.
systems.visualCharacter: orderly, systematic, evenly graded outward — the most 'architectural' spacing available

systems.geometryBasis: Five planets packed inside 0.38 AU, then one distant outlier at 3.11 AU — an 8x jump.
systems.visualCharacter: compact core plus one far-flung body — a system with an outlier

systems.geometryBasis: Remarkably flat and coplanar; five inner planets crowded between 0.09 and 0.25 AU.
systems.visualCharacter: a flat, layered plane — the most 'stratified' system available

systems.geometryBasis: Resonant chain — the outer five are in a 2:4:6:9:12 Laplace resonance.
systems.notes: The resonance is the reason this is the natural candidate for MUSIC.

systems.geometryBasis: Unbroken 3:2 resonant chain for the inner five, then a gap to the sixth.
systems.visualCharacter: an ordered inner sequence, then a break — progression with a discontinuity

systems.geometryBasis: Evenly graded, closely spaced, increasing planet size outward.
systems.visualCharacter: steady outward growth — each shell slightly larger than the last

systems.geometryBasis: Three outer planets in a Laplace resonance (1:2:4); one very close inner planet.
systems.visualCharacter: coupled bodies whose motions are locked to each other

systems.geometryBasis: Only two confirmed planets, both very close in. The nearest star to the Sun.
systems.visualCharacter: sparse, quiet, almost empty — a system defined by what it lacks
systems.notes: Its emptiness is the point; the natural candidate for a MIG with almost no content.

measured._massSource: primary 0.6897 from pscomppars; secondary 0.20 from the Doyle et al. 2011 abstract ("20% and 69% as massive as the sun")
measured._binarySource: Doyle et al. 2011 abstract: "The eclipsing stars are 20% and 69% as massive as the sun, and have an eccentric 41-day orbit."
measured._coplanarSource: Doyle et al. 2011 abstract: "The motions of all three bodies are confined to within 0.5 degree of a single plane."

derived._formula: Kepler's third law, a^3 = M_total * (P/365.25)^2 in AU / solar masses / years
derived._swingMeaning: the small star swings 3.45x wider than the massive one — they are bound, but they do not move equally
derived._planetMeaning: the planet orbits at 3.15x the stellar separation, so the centre of this system is a large empty region
derived._stabilitySource: Holman & Wiegert 1999 critical semi-major axis for P-type orbits, evaluated at e=0. Because the binary is eccentric the true limit is LARGER than this; this is a lower bound only.
derived._sizeMeaning: cube root of the measured mass ratio, used only to size the two stars relative to each other
derived._tempMeaning: follows from 0.20 < 0.69 solar masses on the main sequence; the secondary Teff itself was NOT measured

illustrative._warning: NOT ASTRONOMY. Chosen for rendering because the measured value could not be sourced. Must never be presented as measured.
illustrative._why: Doyle et al. 2011 states the binary orbit IS eccentric but gives no number in any abstract or archive table reachable here, so the orbit is drawn visibly non-circular at a declared value rather than drawn as a circle, which would contradict the published description.
illustrative.orbitSpacingRule: successive 3:2 period ratio, a ∝ P^(2/3), step 1.31037
illustrative._whySpacing: Kepler-16 has exactly ONE measured planet. LOVE has four Minor IGs. Orbit 0 is the real measured orbit; orbits 1-3 are spaced by this declared rule and are NOT measurements.

unverified.binaryEccentricityValue: no numeric value in NASA pscomppars, the ps table, or any fetchable abstract

systems.geometryBasis: CIRCUMBINARY. Two stars of 0.69 and 0.20 solar masses on an eccentric 41-day mutual orbit, derived separation 0.2238 AU. The single measured planet orbits the PAIR at 0.7048 AU — 3.15x the stellar separation — leaving a large dynamically empty centre.
systems.visualCharacter: two unequal centres swinging anti-phase about a shared barycentre, a wide hollow middle where nothing can hold an orbit, then a small number of far, slow bodies
systems.notes: Planet geometry and primary star from pscomppars (Doyle et al. 2011). Secondary mass, binary period, eccentric-ness and 0.5-degree coplanarity from the Doyle et al. 2011 abstract. Binary semi-major axis and barycentre split DERIVED via Kepler third law. Binary eccentricity value remains UNVERIFIED.

gaps.detail: Queried by hostname 'Kepler-90' against pscomppars and got nothing back. It is an 8-planet system and would have been a strong candidate, but it is NOT verified and must not be used until it is.
gaps.action: re-query with correct hostname spelling before use

gaps.detail: The archive returned orbital periods for 5 planets but pl_orbsmax was null for every one. Periods alone cannot place bodies in space without assuming a stellar mass.
gaps.action: either derive from Kepler's third law with a sourced stellar mass, or do not use

gaps.detail: Two MIGs have no exoplanet template yet. Per the brief the fallback is REAL constellation geometry, never an invented system.
